idiom_name: hand-rolled signed cookie: fixed-layout serialization plus HMAC through the OpenSSL EVP signing API, emitted via a Set-Cookie header
implementation_notes: C has no session or cookie abstraction, so the whole structure is hand-written: encode the session struct into a compact, self-describing byte buffer, compute an HMAC over those exact bytes with the EVP signing interface (EVP_DigestSignInit/EVP_DigestSignUpdate/EVP_DigestSignFinal, with HMAC supported as an EVP_PKEY type), base64url-encode payload and tag, and emit them in a Set-Cookie header; on the next request parse the Cookie header, recompute the MAC and compare it in constant time (CRYPTO_memcmp) before decoding. The handwritten form is the right choice in C, but only when you also own the parts a framework would have given you: key storage, constant-time comparison, the cookie grammar, format versioning and the roughly 4 KB cap the browser enforces. Otherwise terminate cookies in a middleware layer and keep conversation state server-side.
pitfalls: The MAC is the only thing between the application and forged session data: compare with CRYPTO_memcmp, never memcmp, which leaks the position of the first differing byte.

Manual parsing of the Cookie header and of the decoded buffer is buffer-overflow territory: bounds-check every length prefix, and treat the decoded bytes as attacker-controlled even after a successful MAC.
Fixed-size buffers silently truncate large state; decide explicitly whether to reject or to move the state server-side, since browsers cap a cookie at roughly 4 KB.
